case_info.scenario: A 25-year-old man taking no regular medications presented to clinic with a 1-month history of skin lesions, which began as small painless papules on his face and progressed to vesicles and pustules over 1 week. Two weeks prior to presentation, he received empirical treatment for herpes simplex virus with a 7-day course of acyclovir (400 mg 3 times daily). However, the lesions enlarged, became verrucous, and new ulcerated, papular lesions appeared on his trunk and extremities; he developed fevers to 39 °C (102.2 °F) and malaise. He had no known history of sexually transmitted infections but reported unprotected sex with multiple male partners. He reported recent exposure to a work colleague with active tuberculosis. At presentation, temperature was 37.4 °C (99.3 °F); respirations, 18/min; heart rate, 80/min; and blood pressure, 102/64 mm Hg; oxygen saturation was 97% on room air. Physical examination revealed crusted, ulcerative, pustular, nodular, and verrucous facial lesions, ulcerative lesions on his back and limbs, and papular lesions across his body (Figure). He had no mucosal lesions or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory results revealed normal hemoglobin level, white blood cell count, glucose level, and liver function. A fourth-generation immunoassay test for HIV was positive, CD4 count was 125 cells/mm3, and HIV viral load was 157 000 copies/mL. A fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS) result was positive. Results of tests for rapid plasma reagin (RPR), human T-lymphotropic virus 1, and tuberculin purified protein derivative were negative. Bacterial culture of the skin lesions grew methicillin-resistantStaphylococcus aureus. Fungal and mycobacterial cultures of the skin lesions were negative, and chest radiography findings were normal.

case_info.explanation: B. Repeat the RPR test with dilution The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that despite the negative RPR test result, the patient’s symptoms, sexual history, positive HIV test result, and positive FTA-ABS result are highly suggestive of syphilis. Skin biopsy (choice A) can provide valuable histopathological information but is invasive and not the first option. Interferon gamma release assay (choice C) is not the appropriate test to diagnose active tuberculosis. Vancomycin (choice D) is incorrect because treatment of methicillin-resistantS aureusfrom a superficial skin culture is not indicated. Malignant syphilis, caused by the spirocheteTreponema pallidum,is a rare and severe form of secondary syphilis characterized by disseminated ulcerative lesions and often accompanied by systemic symptoms of fever, malaise, arthralgias, and myalgias. Skin lesions typically begin as papules and progress to pustules and then to ulcerated, crusted lesions, often with a necrotic center.1Malignant syphilis is more common with immunocompromised conditions such as HIV, use of immunotherapy, malnutrition, diabetes, and alcohol use disorder.2A study of 11 368 HIV-infected patients reported that 1% had syphilis; of those, 7.3% had malignant syphilis.3Histopathology of skin lesions reveals a dense inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrating spirochetes in tissue occurs in approximately 57% of malignant syphilis cases.4 The differential diagnosis of malignant syphilis includes diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis; progressive disseminated histoplasmosis; cryptococcosis, mpox, mycosis fungoides, and tuberculosis verrucosa cutis. There are 2 algorithms to diagnose syphilis, and the choice of algorithm depends on the availability and cost of testing and level of endemicity.5,6The initial test in the reverse algorithm is a treponemal test (eg, FTA-ABS), which detects specific antibodies againstT pallidumand provides a qualitative result (reactive or nonreactive).5,6Because these antibodies can persist lifelong, a positive treponemal test result does not differentiate between newly acquired and previously treated syphilis infection and should be confirmed with a nontreponemal test (eg, RPR or venereal disease research laboratory [VDRL] test). The initial test in the traditional algorithm is a nontreponemal test that assesses serum reactivity to a lecithin-cholesterol-cardiolipin antigen to identify IgG and IgM antibodies in individuals infected withT pallidum.Nontreponemal tests provide semiquantitative results, and the amount of IgM and IgG antibodies reflects the activity of syphilitic infection.5A positive nontreponemal test result should be followed by confirmatory testing with a treponemal test. A nontreponemal test result may be falsely negative when very high syphilis antibody titers interfere with formation of antigen-antibody complex lattice, thereby preventing visible agglutination.7This phenomenon, called the prozone effect, occurs more frequently in patients with HIV, likely due to B-cell dysregulation causing high antibody levels.7When the prozone effect is suspected, the RPR test should be repeated with dilution. Malignant syphilis is treated as secondary syphilis, with a single dose of 2.4 million units of intramuscular benzathine penicillin.8Response to therapy is defined as at least a 4-fold decrease in RPR titer at 12 months,9with rapid disappearance of systemic symptoms and resolution of skin lesions. To evaluate for the prozone effect, a repeat RPR test with dilution was performed and was reactive, with a titer greater than 1:128. A lumbar puncture, performed to rule out neurosyphilis, revealed normal cerebrospinal fluid findings, and the fluid tested negative on VDRL test. Findings on fundoscopic examination to evaluate for ocular syphilis were unremarkable. The patient received a single intramuscular dose of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin and started antiretroviral treatment for HIV with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, lamivudine, and dolutegravir. His skin lesions improved over 2 weeks and resolved after 1 month. At 1 year after therapy, RPR had decreased to 1:8. At most recent follow-up, 24 months after initial presentation, the patient was taking antiretroviral treatment, his CD4 count was 383 cells/mm3, and viral load was undetectable (<40 copies/mL). Skin examination revealed areas of residual postinflammatory hyperpigmentation on his face.

Starting vancomycin alone may miss the underlying cause, such as disseminated mycobacterial or fungal infection, or a severe opportunistic infection like disseminated histoplasmosis or coccidioidomycosis. We need to prioritize a broader diagnostic workup before committing to a single antibiotic.

workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Output Format]
Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:
{
  "mental_demand": <integer 1-5>,
  "performance": <integer 1-5>,
  "effort": <integer 1-5>,
  "frustration": <integer 1-5>,

case_info.explanation: B. Repeat the RPR test with dilution The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that despite the negative RPR test result, the patient’s symptoms, sexual history, positive HIV test result, and positive FTA-ABS result are highly suggestive of syphilis. Skin biopsy (choice A) can provide valuable histopathological information but is invasive and not the first option. Interferon gamma release assay (choice C) is not the appropriate test to diagnose active tuberculosis. Vancomycin (choice D) is incorrect because treatment of methicillin-resistantS aureusfrom a superficial skin culture is not indicated. Malignant syphilis, caused by the spirocheteTreponema pallidum,is a rare and severe form of secondary syphilis characterized by disseminated ulcerative lesions and often accompanied by systemic symptoms of fever, malaise, arthralgias, and myalgias. Skin lesions typically begin as papules and progress to pustules and then to ulcerated, crusted lesions, often with a necrotic center.1Malignant syphilis is more common with immunocompromised conditions such as HIV, use of immunotherapy, malnutrition, diabetes, and alcohol use disorder.2A study of 11 368 HIV-infected patients reported that 1% had syphilis; of those, 7.3% had malignant syphilis.3Histopathology of skin lesions reveals a dense inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrating spirochetes in tissue occurs in approximately 57% of malignant syphilis cases.4 The differential diagnosis of malignant syphilis includes diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis; progressive disseminated histoplasmosis; cryptococcosis, mpox, mycosis fungoides, and tuberculosis verrucosa cutis. There are 2 algorithms to diagnose syphilis, and the choice of algorithm depends on the availability and cost of testing and level of endemicity.5,6The initial test in the reverse algorithm is a treponemal test (eg, FTA-ABS), which detects specific antibodies againstT pallidumand provides a qualitative result (reactive or nonreactive).5,6Because these antibodies can persist lifelong, a positive treponemal test result does not differentiate between newly acquired and previously treated syphilis infection and should be confirmed with a nontreponemal test (eg, RPR or venereal disease research laboratory [VDRL] test). The initial test in the traditional algorithm is a nontreponemal test that assesses serum reactivity to a lecithin-cholesterol-cardiolipin antigen to identify IgG and IgM antibodies in individuals infected withT pallidum.Nontreponemal tests provide semiquantitative results, and the amount of IgM and IgG antibodies reflects the activity of syphilitic infection.5A positive nontreponemal test result should be followed by confirmatory testing with a treponemal test. A nontreponemal test result may be falsely negative when very high syphilis antibody titers interfere with formation of antigen-antibody complex lattice, thereby preventing visible agglutination.7This phenomenon, called the prozone effect, occurs more frequently in patients with HIV, likely due to B-cell dysregulation causing high antibody levels.7When the prozone effect is suspected, the RPR test should be repeated with dilution. Malignant syphilis is treated as secondary syphilis, with a single dose of 2.4 million units of intramuscular benzathine penicillin.8Response to therapy is defined as at least a 4-fold decrease in RPR titer at 12 months,9with rapid disappearance of systemic symptoms and resolution of skin lesions. To evaluate for the prozone effect, a repeat RPR test with dilution was performed and was reactive, with a titer greater than 1:128. A lumbar puncture, performed to rule out neurosyphilis, revealed normal cerebrospinal fluid findings, and the fluid tested negative on VDRL test. Findings on fundoscopic examination to evaluate for ocular syphilis were unremarkable. The patient received a single intramuscular dose of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin and started antiretroviral treatment for HIV with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, lamivudine, and dolutegravir. His skin lesions improved over 2 weeks and resolved after 1 month. At 1 year after therapy, RPR had decreased to 1:8. At most recent follow-up, 24 months after initial presentation, the patient was taking antiretroviral treatment, his CD4 count was 383 cells/mm3, and viral load was undetectable (<40 copies/mL). Skin examination revealed areas of residual postinflammatory hyperpigmentation on his face.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging

       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication

       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.

case_info.explanation: B. Repeat the RPR test with dilution The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that despite the negative RPR test result, the patient’s symptoms, sexual history, positive HIV test result, and positive FTA-ABS result are highly suggestive of syphilis. Skin biopsy (choice A) can provide valuable histopathological information but is invasive and not the first option. Interferon gamma release assay (choice C) is not the appropriate test to diagnose active tuberculosis. Vancomycin (choice D) is incorrect because treatment of methicillin-resistantS aureusfrom a superficial skin culture is not indicated. Malignant syphilis, caused by the spirocheteTreponema pallidum,is a rare and severe form of secondary syphilis characterized by disseminated ulcerative lesions and often accompanied by systemic symptoms of fever, malaise, arthralgias, and myalgias. Skin lesions typically begin as papules and progress to pustules and then to ulcerated, crusted lesions, often with a necrotic center.1Malignant syphilis is more common with immunocompromised conditions such as HIV, use of immunotherapy, malnutrition, diabetes, and alcohol use disorder.2A study of 11 368 HIV-infected patients reported that 1% had syphilis; of those, 7.3% had malignant syphilis.3Histopathology of skin lesions reveals a dense inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrating spirochetes in tissue occurs in approximately 57% of malignant syphilis cases.4 The differential diagnosis of malignant syphilis includes diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis; progressive disseminated histoplasmosis; cryptococcosis, mpox, mycosis fungoides, and tuberculosis verrucosa cutis. There are 2 algorithms to diagnose syphilis, and the choice of algorithm depends on the availability and cost of testing and level of endemicity.5,6The initial test in the reverse algorithm is a treponemal test (eg, FTA-ABS), which detects specific antibodies againstT pallidumand provides a qualitative result (reactive or nonreactive).5,6Because these antibodies can persist lifelong, a positive treponemal test result does not differentiate between newly acquired and previously treated syphilis infection and should be confirmed with a nontreponemal test (eg, RPR or venereal disease research laboratory [VDRL] test). The initial test in the traditional algorithm is a nontreponemal test that assesses serum reactivity to a lecithin-cholesterol-cardiolipin antigen to identify IgG and IgM antibodies in individuals infected withT pallidum.Nontreponemal tests provide semiquantitative results, and the amount of IgM and IgG antibodies reflects the activity of syphilitic infection.5A positive nontreponemal test result should be followed by confirmatory testing with a treponemal test. A nontreponemal test result may be falsely negative when very high syphilis antibody titers interfere with formation of antigen-antibody complex lattice, thereby preventing visible agglutination.7This phenomenon, called the prozone effect, occurs more frequently in patients with HIV, likely due to B-cell dysregulation causing high antibody levels.7When the prozone effect is suspected, the RPR test should be repeated with dilution. Malignant syphilis is treated as secondary syphilis, with a single dose of 2.4 million units of intramuscular benzathine penicillin.8Response to therapy is defined as at least a 4-fold decrease in RPR titer at 12 months,9with rapid disappearance of systemic symptoms and resolution of skin lesions. To evaluate for the prozone effect, a repeat RPR test with dilution was performed and was reactive, with a titer greater than 1:128. A lumbar puncture, performed to rule out neurosyphilis, revealed normal cerebrospinal fluid findings, and the fluid tested negative on VDRL test. Findings on fundoscopic examination to evaluate for ocular syphilis were unremarkable. The patient received a single intramuscular dose of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin and started antiretroviral treatment for HIV with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, lamivudine, and dolutegravir. His skin lesions improved over 2 weeks and resolved after 1 month. At 1 year after therapy, RPR had decreased to 1:8. At most recent follow-up, 24 months after initial presentation, the patient was taking antiretroviral treatment, his CD4 count was 383 cells/mm3, and viral load was undetectable (<40 copies/mL). Skin examination revealed areas of residual postinflammatory hyperpigmentation on his face.

messages.content:
You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 25-year-old man taking no regular medications presented to clinic with a 1-month history of skin lesions, which began as small painless papules on his face and progressed to vesicles and pustules over 1 week. Two weeks prior to presentation, he received empirical treatment for herpes simplex virus with a 7-day course of acyclovir (400 mg 3 times daily). However, the lesions enlarged, became verrucous, and new ulcerated, papular lesions appeared on his trunk and extremities; he developed fevers to 39 °C (102.2 °F) and malaise. He had no known history of sexually transmitted infections but reported unprotected sex with multiple male partners. He reported recent exposure to a work colleague with active tuberculosis. At presentation, temperature was 37.4 °C (99.3 °F); respirations, 18/min; heart rate, 80/min; and blood pressure, 102/64 mm Hg; oxygen saturation was 97% on room air. Physical examination revealed crusted, ulcerative, pustular, nodular, and verrucous facial lesions, ulcerative lesions on his back and limbs, and papular lesions across his body (Figure). He had no mucosal lesions or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory results revealed normal hemoglobin level, white blood cell count, glucose level, and liver function. A fourth-generation immunoassay test for HIV was positive, CD4 count was 125 cells/mm3, and HIV viral load was 157 000 copies/mL. A fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS) result was positive. Results of tests for rapid plasma reagin (RPR), human T-lymphotropic virus 1, and tuberculin purified protein derivative were negative. Bacterial culture of the skin lesions grew methicillin-resistantStaphylococcus aureus. Fungal and mycobacterial cultures of the skin lesions were negative, and chest radiography findings were normal.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

The patient's immunocompromised state due to HIV also increases the risk of severe infections, necessitating aggressive treatment.

While MRSA coverage is important, the patient's disseminated, progressive lesions with fevers and HIV diagnosis point to a more systemic process. Starting vancomycin alone may miss the underlying cause, such as disseminated mycobacterial or fungal infection, or a severe opportunistic infection like disseminated histoplasmosis or coccidioidomycosis. We need to prioritize a broader diagnostic workup before committing to a single antibiotic.

While I acknowledge the concern regarding the potential for systemic infections, the immediate presence of MRSA in the skin cultures necessitates starting vancomycin to address the bacterial infection. The patient's immunocompromised state due to HIV heightens the urgency of treating the known infection rather than delaying for broader diagnostics. Nonetheless, I agree that we should subsequently evaluate for other opportunistic infections as part of a comprehensive management plan.

I agree that starting vancomycin is appropriate for the MRSA superinfection, but given the verrucous morphology, systemic symptoms, and positive FTA-ABS, we must simultaneously treat for disseminated syphilis, which can mimic many skin conditions in HIV. Initiating penicillin G for neurosyphilis should be considered alongside the vancomycin, as the negative RPR does not rule out active disease in this setting.

While I appreciate the importance of ruling out opportunistic infections and the implications of syphilis given the positive FTA-ABS, the immediate necessity is to address the confirmed MRSA. We can consider initiating treatment for syphilis after starting vancomycin, as the patient's acute condition with active MRSA requires urgent intervention.

Given the HIV diagnosis and negative PPD, we should urgently obtain a biopsy of a lesion for histopathology and special stains while starting antibiotics.

[Clinician's current statement]
I recognize the value in obtaining a biopsy to further assess the lesions, especially given the atypical presentation and the immunocompromised status of the patient. However, I still believe that the immediate priority is to start vancomycin for the confirmed MRSA infection, as it poses a significant risk to the patient's health. We can pursue the biopsy concurrently with the initiation of antibiotic therapy.

Respond directly to this statement.

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 9.5. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Output Format]
Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:
{
  "mental_demand": <integer 1-5>,
  "performance": <integer 1-5>,
  "effort": <integer 1-5>,
  "frustration": <integer 1-5>,
  "overall_workload": <mean of mental_demand, performance, effort, and frustration,

case_info.explanation: B. Repeat the RPR test with dilution The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that despite the negative RPR test result, the patient’s symptoms, sexual history, positive HIV test result, and positive FTA-ABS result are highly suggestive of syphilis. Skin biopsy (choice A) can provide valuable histopathological information but is invasive and not the first option. Interferon gamma release assay (choice C) is not the appropriate test to diagnose active tuberculosis. Vancomycin (choice D) is incorrect because treatment of methicillin-resistantS aureusfrom a superficial skin culture is not indicated. Malignant syphilis, caused by the spirocheteTreponema pallidum,is a rare and severe form of secondary syphilis characterized by disseminated ulcerative lesions and often accompanied by systemic symptoms of fever, malaise, arthralgias, and myalgias. Skin lesions typically begin as papules and progress to pustules and then to ulcerated, crusted lesions, often with a necrotic center.1Malignant syphilis is more common with immunocompromised conditions such as HIV, use of immunotherapy, malnutrition, diabetes, and alcohol use disorder.2A study of 11 368 HIV-infected patients reported that 1% had syphilis; of those, 7.3% had malignant syphilis.3Histopathology of skin lesions reveals a dense inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrating spirochetes in tissue occurs in approximately 57% of malignant syphilis cases.4 The differential diagnosis of malignant syphilis includes diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis; progressive disseminated histoplasmosis; cryptococcosis, mpox, mycosis fungoides, and tuberculosis verrucosa cutis. There are 2 algorithms to diagnose syphilis, and the choice of algorithm depends on the availability and cost of testing and level of endemicity.5,6The initial test in the reverse algorithm is a treponemal test (eg, FTA-ABS), which detects specific antibodies againstT pallidumand provides a qualitative result (reactive or nonreactive).5,6Because these antibodies can persist lifelong, a positive treponemal test result does not differentiate between newly acquired and previously treated syphilis infection and should be confirmed with a nontreponemal test (eg, RPR or venereal disease research laboratory [VDRL] test). The initial test in the traditional algorithm is a nontreponemal test that assesses serum reactivity to a lecithin-cholesterol-cardiolipin antigen to identify IgG and IgM antibodies in individuals infected withT pallidum.Nontreponemal tests provide semiquantitative results, and the amount of IgM and IgG antibodies reflects the activity of syphilitic infection.5A positive nontreponemal test result should be followed by confirmatory testing with a treponemal test. A nontreponemal test result may be falsely negative when very high syphilis antibody titers interfere with formation of antigen-antibody complex lattice, thereby preventing visible agglutination.7This phenomenon, called the prozone effect, occurs more frequently in patients with HIV, likely due to B-cell dysregulation causing high antibody levels.7When the prozone effect is suspected, the RPR test should be repeated with dilution. Malignant syphilis is treated as secondary syphilis, with a single dose of 2.4 million units of intramuscular benzathine penicillin.8Response to therapy is defined as at least a 4-fold decrease in RPR titer at 12 months,9with rapid disappearance of systemic symptoms and resolution of skin lesions. To evaluate for the prozone effect, a repeat RPR test with dilution was performed and was reactive, with a titer greater than 1:128. A lumbar puncture, performed to rule out neurosyphilis, revealed normal cerebrospinal fluid findings, and the fluid tested negative on VDRL test. Findings on fundoscopic examination to evaluate for ocular syphilis were unremarkable. The patient received a single intramuscular dose of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin and started antiretroviral treatment for HIV with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, lamivudine, and dolutegravir. His skin lesions improved over 2 weeks and resolved after 1 month. At 1 year after therapy, RPR had decreased to 1:8. At most recent follow-up, 24 months after initial presentation, the patient was taking antiretroviral treatment, his CD4 count was 383 cells/mm3, and viral load was undetectable (<40 copies/mL). Skin examination revealed areas of residual postinflammatory hyperpigmentation on his face.

case_info.explanation: B. Repeat the RPR test with dilution The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that despite the negative RPR test result, the patient’s symptoms, sexual history, positive HIV test result, and positive FTA-ABS result are highly suggestive of syphilis. Skin biopsy (choice A) can provide valuable histopathological information but is invasive and not the first option. Interferon gamma release assay (choice C) is not the appropriate test to diagnose active tuberculosis. Vancomycin (choice D) is incorrect because treatment of methicillin-resistantS aureusfrom a superficial skin culture is not indicated. Malignant syphilis, caused by the spirocheteTreponema pallidum,is a rare and severe form of secondary syphilis characterized by disseminated ulcerative lesions and often accompanied by systemic symptoms of fever, malaise, arthralgias, and myalgias. Skin lesions typically begin as papules and progress to pustules and then to ulcerated, crusted lesions, often with a necrotic center.1Malignant syphilis is more common with immunocompromised conditions such as HIV, use of immunotherapy, malnutrition, diabetes, and alcohol use disorder.2A study of 11 368 HIV-infected patients reported that 1% had syphilis; of those, 7.3% had malignant syphilis.3Histopathology of skin lesions reveals a dense inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrating spirochetes in tissue occurs in approximately 57% of malignant syphilis cases.4 The differential diagnosis of malignant syphilis includes diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis; progressive disseminated histoplasmosis; cryptococcosis, mpox, mycosis fungoides, and tuberculosis verrucosa cutis. There are 2 algorithms to diagnose syphilis, and the choice of algorithm depends on the availability and cost of testing and level of endemicity.5,6The initial test in the reverse algorithm is a treponemal test (eg, FTA-ABS), which detects specific antibodies againstT pallidumand provides a qualitative result (reactive or nonreactive).5,6Because these antibodies can persist lifelong, a positive treponemal test result does not differentiate between newly acquired and previously treated syphilis infection and should be confirmed with a nontreponemal test (eg, RPR or venereal disease research laboratory [VDRL] test). The initial test in the traditional algorithm is a nontreponemal test that assesses serum reactivity to a lecithin-cholesterol-cardiolipin antigen to identify IgG and IgM antibodies in individuals infected withT pallidum.Nontreponemal tests provide semiquantitative results, and the amount of IgM and IgG antibodies reflects the activity of syphilitic infection.5A positive nontreponemal test result should be followed by confirmatory testing with a treponemal test. A nontreponemal test result may be falsely negative when very high syphilis antibody titers interfere with formation of antigen-antibody complex lattice, thereby preventing visible agglutination.7This phenomenon, called the prozone effect, occurs more frequently in patients with HIV, likely due to B-cell dysregulation causing high antibody levels.7When the prozone effect is suspected, the RPR test should be repeated with dilution. Malignant syphilis is treated as secondary syphilis, with a single dose of 2.4 million units of intramuscular benzathine penicillin.8Response to therapy is defined as at least a 4-fold decrease in RPR titer at 12 months,9with rapid disappearance of systemic symptoms and resolution of skin lesions. To evaluate for the prozone effect, a repeat RPR test with dilution was performed and was reactive, with a titer greater than 1:128. A lumbar puncture, performed to rule out neurosyphilis, revealed normal cerebrospinal fluid findings, and the fluid tested negative on VDRL test. Findings on fundoscopic examination to evaluate for ocular syphilis were unremarkable. The patient received a single intramuscular dose of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin and started antiretroviral treatment for HIV with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, lamivudine, and dolutegravir. His skin lesions improved over 2 weeks and resolved after 1 month. At 1 year after therapy, RPR had decreased to 1:8. At most recent follow-up, 24 months after initial presentation, the patient was taking antiretroviral treatment, his CD4 count was 383 cells/mm3, and viral load was undetectable (<40 copies/mL). Skin examination revealed areas of residual postinflammatory hyperpigmentation on his face.

Repeat the RPR test with dilution The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that despite the negative RPR test result, the patient’s symptoms, sexual history, positive HIV test result, and positive FTA-ABS result are highly suggestive of syphilis. Skin biopsy (choice A) can provide valuable histopathological information but is invasive and not the first option. Interferon gamma release assay (choice C) is not the appropriate test to diagnose active tuberculosis. Vancomycin (choice D) is incorrect because treatment of methicillin-resistantS aureusfrom a superficial skin culture is not indicated. Malignant syphilis, caused by the spirocheteTreponema pallidum,is a rare and severe form of secondary syphilis characterized by disseminated ulcerative lesions and often accompanied by systemic symptoms of fever, malaise, arthralgias, and myalgias. Skin lesions typically begin as papules and progress to pustules and then to ulcerated, crusted lesions, often with a necrotic center.1Malignant syphilis is more common with immunocompromised conditions such as HIV, use of immunotherapy, malnutrition, diabetes, and alcohol use disorder.2A study of 11 368 HIV-infected patients reported that 1% had syphilis; of those, 7.3% had malignant syphilis.3Histopathology of skin lesions reveals a dense inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrating spirochetes in tissue occurs in approximately 57% of malignant syphilis cases.4 The differential diagnosis of malignant syphilis includes diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis; progressive disseminated histoplasmosis; cryptococcosis, mpox, mycosis fungoides, and tuberculosis verrucosa cutis. There are 2 algorithms to diagnose syphilis, and the choice of algorithm depends on the availability and cost of testing and level of endemicity.5,6The initial test in the reverse algorithm is a treponemal test (eg, FTA-ABS), which detects specific antibodies againstT pallidumand provides a qualitative result (reactive or nonreactive).5,6Because these antibodies can persist lifelong, a positive treponemal test result does not differentiate between newly acquired and previously treated syphilis infection and should be confirmed with a nontreponemal test (eg, RPR or venereal disease research laboratory [VDRL] test). The initial test in the traditional algorithm is a nontreponemal test that assesses serum reactivity to a lecithin-cholesterol-cardiolipin antigen to identify IgG and IgM antibodies in individuals infected withT pallidum.Nontreponemal tests provide semiquantitative results, and the amount of IgM and IgG antibodies reflects the activity of syphilitic infection.5A positive nontreponemal test result should be followed by confirmatory testing with a treponemal test. A nontreponemal test result may be falsely negative when very high syphilis antibody titers interfere with formation of antigen-antibody complex lattice, thereby preventing visible agglutination.7This phenomenon, called the prozone effect, occurs more frequently in patients with HIV, likely due to B-cell dysregulation causing high antibody levels.7When the prozone effect is suspected, the RPR test should be repeated with dilution. Malignant syphilis is treated as secondary syphilis, with a single dose of 2.4 million units of intramuscular benzathine penicillin.8Response to therapy is defined as at least a 4-fold decrease in RPR titer at 12 months,9with rapid disappearance of systemic symptoms and resolution of skin lesions. To evaluate for the prozone effect, a repeat RPR test with dilution was performed and was reactive, with a titer greater than 1:128. A lumbar puncture, performed to rule out neurosyphilis, revealed normal cerebrospinal fluid findings, and the fluid tested negative on VDRL test. Findings on fundoscopic examination to evaluate for ocular syphilis were unremarkable. The patient received a single intramuscular dose of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin and started antiretroviral treatment for HIV with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, lamivudine, and dolutegravir. His skin lesions improved over 2 weeks and resolved after 1 month. At 1 year after therapy, RPR had decreased to 1:8. At most recent follow-up, 24 months after initial presentation, the patient was taking antiretroviral treatment, his CD4 count was 383 cells/mm3, and viral load was undetectable (<40 copies/mL). Skin examination revealed areas of residual postinflammatory hyperpigmentation on his face.

case_info.explanation: B. Repeat the RPR test with dilution The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that despite the negative RPR test result, the patient’s symptoms, sexual history, positive HIV test result, and positive FTA-ABS result are highly suggestive of syphilis. Skin biopsy (choice A) can provide valuable histopathological information but is invasive and not the first option. Interferon gamma release assay (choice C) is not the appropriate test to diagnose active tuberculosis. Vancomycin (choice D) is incorrect because treatment of methicillin-resistantS aureusfrom a superficial skin culture is not indicated. Malignant syphilis, caused by the spirocheteTreponema pallidum,is a rare and severe form of secondary syphilis characterized by disseminated ulcerative lesions and often accompanied by systemic symptoms of fever, malaise, arthralgias, and myalgias. Skin lesions typically begin as papules and progress to pustules and then to ulcerated, crusted lesions, often with a necrotic center.1Malignant syphilis is more common with immunocompromised conditions such as HIV, use of immunotherapy, malnutrition, diabetes, and alcohol use disorder.2A study of 11 368 HIV-infected patients reported that 1% had syphilis; of those, 7.3% had malignant syphilis.3Histopathology of skin lesions reveals a dense inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrating spirochetes in tissue occurs in approximately 57% of malignant syphilis cases.4 The differential diagnosis of malignant syphilis includes diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis; progressive disseminated histoplasmosis; cryptococcosis, mpox, mycosis fungoides, and tuberculosis verrucosa cutis. There are 2 algorithms to diagnose syphilis, and the choice of algorithm depends on the availability and cost of testing and level of endemicity.5,6The initial test in the reverse algorithm is a treponemal test (eg, FTA-ABS), which detects specific antibodies againstT pallidumand provides a qualitative result (reactive or nonreactive).5,6Because these antibodies can persist lifelong, a positive treponemal test result does not differentiate between newly acquired and previously treated syphilis infection and should be confirmed with a nontreponemal test (eg, RPR or venereal disease research laboratory [VDRL] test). The initial test in the traditional algorithm is a nontreponemal test that assesses serum reactivity to a lecithin-cholesterol-cardiolipin antigen to identify IgG and IgM antibodies in individuals infected withT pallidum.Nontreponemal tests provide semiquantitative results, and the amount of IgM and IgG antibodies reflects the activity of syphilitic infection.5A positive nontreponemal test result should be followed by confirmatory testing with a treponemal test. A nontreponemal test result may be falsely negative when very high syphilis antibody titers interfere with formation of antigen-antibody complex lattice, thereby preventing visible agglutination.7This phenomenon, called the prozone effect, occurs more frequently in patients with HIV, likely due to B-cell dysregulation causing high antibody levels.7When the prozone effect is suspected, the RPR test should be repeated with dilution. Malignant syphilis is treated as secondary syphilis, with a single dose of 2.4 million units of intramuscular benzathine penicillin.8Response to therapy is defined as at least a 4-fold decrease in RPR titer at 12 months,9with rapid disappearance of systemic symptoms and resolution of skin lesions. To evaluate for the prozone effect, a repeat RPR test with dilution was performed and was reactive, with a titer greater than 1:128. A lumbar puncture, performed to rule out neurosyphilis, revealed normal cerebrospinal fluid findings, and the fluid tested negative on VDRL test. Findings on fundoscopic examination to evaluate for ocular syphilis were unremarkable. The patient received a single intramuscular dose of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin and started antiretroviral treatment for HIV with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, lamivudine, and dolutegravir. His skin lesions improved over 2 weeks and resolved after 1 month. At 1 year after therapy, RPR had decreased to 1:8. At most recent follow-up, 24 months after initial presentation, the patient was taking antiretroviral treatment, his CD4 count was 383 cells/mm3, and viral load was undetectable (<40 copies/mL). Skin examination revealed areas of residual postinflammatory hyperpigmentation on his face.
